title: How to profile a Java application — JFR (Java Flight Recorder) for low-overhead production profiling, JMC (Java Mission Control) for analysis, VisualVM for heap/thread inspection, async-profiler for CPU/allocation profiling?
shortTitle: How to profile a Java application?

s1_definition.profdef: Profiling means measuring where a running application spends its time and memory so you can find bottlenecks with data instead of guesswork. Java Flight Recorder (JFR) is a built-in, very low-overhead recorder that captures detailed runtime events and is safe to run in production. Java Mission Control (JMC) is the desktop tool that opens and analyzes JFR recordings. VisualVM is a free tool for live heap, thread, and CPU inspection. async-profiler is a sampling profiler that produces accurate CPU and allocation flame graphs with minimal overhead.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India's branch is slow and you want to know why without disrupting customers. Profiling is like quietly observing the branch with a stopwatch and a notebook. JFR is a discreet security camera that records what every counter is doing all day with almost no effect on the staff, safe to leave running even during peak hours. JMC is the review room where you play back that footage and spot that the loan desk is the bottleneck. VisualVM is walking the floor right now to see which counters are busy this moment. async-profiler is a heat-map of the whole branch showing exactly which tasks consume the most effort. Together they tell you precisely where the slowdown is, so you fix the right counter instead of guessing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Profile with data, not hunches — JFR records cheaply in production, JMC analyzes it, VisualVM inspects live, and async-profiler gives CPU and allocation flame graphs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Profiling means measuring where a running application spends its time and memory so you can find bottlenecks with data instead of guesswork. Java Flight Recorder (JFR) is a built-in, very low-overhead recorder that captures detailed runtime events and is safe to run in production. Java Mission Control (JMC) is the desktop tool that opens and analyzes JFR recordings. VisualVM is a free tool for live heap, thread, and CPU inspection. async-profiler is a sampling profiler that produces accurate CPU and allocation flame graphs with minimal overhead.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose National Bank of India's branch is slow and you want to know why without disrupting customers. Profiling is like quietly observing the branch with a stopwatch and a notebook. JFR is a discreet security camera that records what every counter is doing all day with almost no effect on the staff, safe to leave running even during peak hours. JMC is the review room where you play back that footage and spot that the loan desk is the bottleneck. VisualVM is walking the floor right now to see which counters are busy this moment. async-profiler is a heat-map of the whole branch showing exactly which tasks consume the most effort. Together they tell you precisely where the slowdown is, so you fix the right counter instead of guessing.

**One line to remember:** Profile with data, not hunches — JFR records cheaply in production, JMC analyzes it, VisualVM inspects live, and async-profiler gives CPU and allocation flame graphs.

sections.s2_technical:
Java Flight Recorder is built into the JDK and records a stream of events — method execution samples, allocations, GC pauses, lock contention, thread states, I/O — with overhead usually around one percent, which is why it is safe in production. You start a recording at launch with `-XX:StartFlightRecording` or attach to a running process with `jcmd <pid> JFR.start`. The result is a `.jfr` file you analyze later. The key strength of JFR is that it is always-affordable, so you can capture the exact moment a problem happens in production rather than trying to reproduce it in a lab.

Java Mission Control is the analysis tool that opens `.jfr` files. It gives you ready-made views: a hot-methods list showing where CPU time went, an allocation view showing which code allocates the most, a GC view, a lock-contention view, and an automated analysis that flags likely problems. You use JMC to turn a raw recording into a diagnosis, for example "eighty percent of CPU is in BigDecimal division inside the interest loop."

VisualVM is a free, lightweight tool for live inspection. You attach it to a running JVM and watch heap usage, thread states, and a sampling CPU profiler in real time. It is excellent for quick, interactive investigation on a development or staging machine, and it can take and compare heap dumps to help with memory issues.

async-profiler is a low-overhead sampling profiler especially good at CPU and allocation profiling, and it produces flame graphs. A flame graph is a picture where the width of each box shows how much time (or allocation) a method and its callees consumed, so the widest boxes are your biggest costs. Because it samples using operating-system and JVM mechanisms, it avoids the "safepoint bias" that can mislead simpler profilers. A senior nuance: always profile under a realistic load and after JIT warm-up, measure the right thing (CPU time for compute bottlenecks, allocation for GC pressure, wall-clock for latency including waiting), and change one thing at a time, re-profiling after each change to confirm it actually helped.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's end-of-day statement generation got slow, and the team argued about whether the database or the Java code was to blame. This is exactly where profiling settles the debate with data — a JFR recording shows precisely where the time goes.

Problem 2 — We cannot reproduce the slowness in a test environment; it only happens under real production load. This is exactly why JFR matters — its overhead is low enough to leave recording in production and capture the real event.

Problem 3 — We suspect excessive object allocation is driving GC pressure during statement generation. This is exactly what async-profiler's allocation flame graph reveals — which method allocates the most.

Our mini-project builds a `ProfilingDemo` statement-generation workload with a deliberately expensive hot path, plus a `ProfilerLauncher` helper that starts and stops a JFR recording programmatically via `jcmd`-style diagnostic commands and reports where to analyze it. The reader runs it with JFR enabled and opens the resulting `.jfr` in JMC, and optionally attaches async-profiler.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
jvm-profiling-demo/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/
            ├── ProfilingDemo.java         (main runnable workload)
            ├── StatementGenerator.java    (the hot, allocation-heavy path)
            └── ProfilerLauncher.java      (starts/stops JFR programmatically)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/jvm/*.java

# Simplest: start JFR at launch (low overhead, production-safe)
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=/tmp/bank.jfr,settings=profile \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.ProfilingDemo

# Attach JFR to an ALREADY running process (find pid with jps)
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=live filename=/tmp/live.jfr settings=profile
jcmd <pid> JFR.stop name=live

# Analyze the recording in Java Mission Control (GUI): File > Open > bank.jfr
# CPU flame graph + allocation flame graph with async-profiler:
java -agentpath:/path/to/libasyncProfiler.so=start,event=cpu,file=/tmp/cpu.html \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.ProfilingDemo
java -agentpath:/path/to/libasyncProfiler.so=start,event=alloc,file=/tmp/alloc.html \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.ProfilingDemo

# VisualVM: launch visualvm, attach to the pid, watch Threads + Sampler tabs
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: 200,000 accounts, each requiring a 20-line statement string and a fee calculation; JFR recording enabled.

Step 1 — The ProfilerLauncher starts a JFR recording with the "profile" settings, which capture method samples, allocations, and GC events at low overhead.

Step 2 — The StatementGenerator loops over 200,000 accounts. For each, it builds a statement by concatenating strings in an inner loop, which creates many temporary String objects, and computes a fee with BigDecimal.

Step 3 — While this runs, JFR continuously records samples. It notes that most CPU time is spent inside string concatenation and that this same code allocates the most objects, driving GC activity.

Step 4 — When the workload finishes, the launcher stops the recording and JFR writes the `.jfr` file to disk. The run logs where to find it.

Step 5 — The engineer opens the file in Java Mission Control. The hot-methods view shows `StatementGenerator.generateForAllAccounts` dominating CPU, and the allocation view shows the String concatenation as the top allocator. The automated analysis flags inefficient string handling.

Step 6 — Guided by the data, the fix is to replace the string concatenation in a loop with a StringBuilder, which eliminates most allocations. Re-profiling confirms CPU and GC pressure drop, proving the change helped rather than assuming it.

Final output:

```

2026-10-31 23:16:04 [INFO] JFR recording stopped
2026-10-31 23:16:04 [INFO] Open /tmp/bank-statements.jfr in Java Mission Control to analyze hot methods & allocations
# In JMC: Hot Methods -> StatementGenerator.generateForAllAccounts 81% CPU

    Pre:  count >= 0
    Post: returns total fees; allocates heavily (the bug to find)

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Profiling means finding where an application actually spends its time and memory using measurement, not intuition, and the first rule I follow is to never optimize based on a guess. The tool I reach for first is Java Flight Recorder, which is built into the JDK and records a rich stream of events — method samples, allocations, GC pauses, lock contention — with overhead of roughly one percent. That low overhead is the whole point, because it means I can leave it running in production and capture a problem the moment it happens, rather than failing to reproduce it in a test environment. I start it at launch with StartFlightRecording or attach to a running process with jcmd, and I get a dot-jfr file.

To analyze that file I use Java Mission Control, which opens the recording and gives me ready-made views: the hottest methods by CPU, which code allocates the most, GC behavior, and lock contention, plus an automated analysis that flags likely issues. For quick live triage on a development or staging machine I use VisualVM, which attaches to a running JVM and shows heap, threads, and a sampling CPU profiler in real time. And when I want precise CPU or allocation flame graphs, I use async-profiler, where the widest boxes in the flame graph are immediately my biggest costs, and it avoids the safepoint bias that can mislead simpler profilers.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this exact toolkit resolved a real argument. Our end-of-day statement generation had become slow, and the team was split on whether the database or the Java code was at fault. I captured a JFR recording in production, opened it in JMC, and the hot-methods view showed that over eighty percent of the CPU was being spent building statement strings by concatenation inside a loop, which was also the top allocator and the source of our GC pressure. The database was innocent. I replaced the concatenation with a StringBuilder, re-profiled under the same load to confirm CPU and allocation both dropped, and only then shipped it. The discipline that made it work was profiling under realistic load after warm-up, measuring the right dimension, and changing one thing at a time while re-profiling to prove the fix.
